usage: 요리(料理) is the noun 'a dish/cuisine'; 하다 makes it a verb, which is why the negative splits as 요리(를) 안 해요
집에서 marks the location with -에서 (the place an action happens), not -에 — a very common particle slip
the dish you make takes the object particle -을/를: 한식을 요리해요
잘하다 ('do well') is written as one word; 요리를 잘해요 means 'I cook well'
examples: 엄마가 요리해요.
Mom is cooking.
Bare subject + verb — the simplest 요-form sentence, built on the stem 요리하 + 여요 → 요리해요
주말에는 집에서 직접 요리해요.
On weekends I cook at home myself.
직접 ('in person, oneself') stresses that you do it yourself rather than buying or ordering
오늘은 피곤해서 요리 못 해요.
I am tired today, so I can't cook.
Real-life excuse — note 못 splits the compound: 요리 못 해요, never 못 요리해요
nuance: 요리하다 (料理하다, 料 'handle/measure' + 理 'arrange/manage') means to actually prepare a dish — chopping, seasoning, applying heat — so it carries a sense of real cooking, not just touching the stove. Contrast it with 끓이다 ('boil', e.g. 라면을 끓이다 for instant noodles) and 데우다 ('reheat'): a Korean would say 라면을 끓여요, not 라면을 요리해요, because boiling ramyeon barely counts as 요리. As a 하다-verb the stem 요리하 + 여요 contracts to 요리해요, and because 요리 is a separable noun the negative and 못 wedge between the two parts: 요리 안 해요, 요리 못 해요. The English-speaker trap is mirroring 'I cook dinner' as 저녁을 요리해요 (fine) but then saying 저녁 안 요리해요 — wrong; it must be 저녁 요리 안 해요 or 저녁을 안 만들어요. Also note that for a quick everyday meal Koreans very often just say 밥을 하다 ('do rice' = make a meal) rather than 요리하다.

mistakes: Saying 못 요리해요 for 'I can't cook' — 요리하다 is noun(요리)+하다, so 못 must go right before 하다: 요리 못 해요.
Using 요리하다 for boiling ramyeon or just reheating soup — Koreans use 끓이다 or 데우다; 요리하다 implies actually making a dish.
Writing the negative as 안 요리해요 — the standard split form is 요리 안 해요 (the noun, then 안, then 해요).

usage: 빨래 is a pure-Korean noun meaning both 'the washing (action)' and 'the laundry (items)'; the verb is 빨래(를) 하다
널다 ('hang out to dry') is the natural next step after washing; 빨래를 널어요
개다 means 'fold' for laundry/blankets — not 접다, which is for paper; 빨래를 개요
손(hand)+빨래 = washing by hand, as opposed to using the 세탁기 (washing machine)
examples: 빨래해요.
I'm doing laundry.
Minimal sentence: stem 빨래하 + 여요 → 빨래해요, the everyday spoken form
날씨가 좋으니까 빨래할까요?
The weather's nice, so shall we do laundry?
-(으)니까 gives the reason for a suggestion; 빨래할까요? proposes doing it
세탁기가 고장 나서 빨래 못 해요.
The washer broke, so I can't do laundry.
고장 나다 = 'break down'; 못 splits the compound as 빨래 못 해요
nuance: 빨래하다 specifically means to wash clothes/fabric, and the noun 빨래 doubly refers to both the act and the pile of clothes themselves (빨래가 많아요 = 'there's a lot of laundry'). Don't confuse it with neighbors that all touch 'wash': 씻다 is washing your body or hands (손을 씻다), 설거지하다 is washing dishes, and 빨다 is the raw verb 'to scrub/wash (cloth)' from which 빨래 derives — so 양말을 빨다 ('wash socks') and 빨래하다 overlap, but 빨래하다 names the whole chore. As a noun+하다 compound, 안 and 못 insert before 하다: 빨래 안 해요, 빨래 못 해요. The classic English-speaker error is reaching for 씻다 because English says 'wash my clothes' the same way as 'wash my hands' — but 옷을 씻다 sounds wrong to Koreans; say 옷을 빨다 or 빨래해요. Habitual collocations: 빨래를 하다 → 널다(hang) → 개다(fold).

Using 접다 to 'fold laundry' — paper is 접다, but clothes and blankets are 개다: 빨래를 개요.
Putting 못 first as 못 빨래해요 — the correct split is 빨래 못 해요 because 빨래+하다 is a separable compound.

usage: 고장 나다 = 'break down'; the broken thing is the object: 시계를 고쳐요
고치다 reaches beyond objects to habits and faults — 나쁜 버릇을 고치다
for errors in writing/answers, 고치다 means 'correct': 답을 고쳐요
고치다 even covers curing sickness; 의사가 병을 고쳐요 ('the doctor cures the illness')
examples: 시계를 고쳐요.
I fix the watch.
Plain object + verb; stem 고치 + 어요 → 고쳐요 (이+어 contracts to 여)
고장 난 의자를 직접 고쳤어요.
I fixed the broken chair myself.
고장 난 is the past-modifier 'broken'; 고쳤어요 is the past tense
이 가방 좀 고쳐 주세요.
Could you fix this bag for me?
좀 softens the request and 고쳐 주세요 asks someone to do it for your benefit
nuance: 고치다 is wonderfully broad: it repairs broken objects (자전거를 고치다), corrects mistakes (답을 고치다), reforms bad habits (버릇을 고치다), and even cures illness (병을 고치다) — the unifying idea is 'restore something faulty to a good state'. The sharp line to learn is 고치다 vs 바꾸다: 고치다 keeps the SAME thing and makes it work again, while 바꾸다 swaps it for a DIFFERENT one. If your phone is buggy, 핸드폰을 고쳐요 means repair this phone, but 핸드폰을 바꿔요 means get a new phone. A more formal/technical synonym is 수리하다 (修理, used for appliances/cars on signs and receipts: 수리 센터), and for software/policy you'll hear 수정하다 (修正, 'revise'). The verb is regular: 고치 + 어요 → 고쳐요, past 고쳤어요. English-speaker pitfall: don't overextend the English 'fix' meaning 'arrange/decide' (as in 'fix a date') — that's 정하다, not 고치다. 날짜를 고치다 would mean 'change the already-set date', a different idea.

usage: for currency exchange Koreans say 돈을 바꾸다 / 환전하다; 달러로 바꿔요 ('change into dollars')
바꾸다 covers swapping positions with someone: 저랑 자리 좀 바꿔 주세요
the idiom for changing your decision/mind — 마음을 바꿨어요 ('I changed my mind')
the thing you get takes -(으)로: 큰 사이즈로 바꿔 주세요 ('change it to a large')
examples: 이름을 바꿔요.
I change my name.
Simple object + verb; stem 바꾸 + 어요 → 바꿔요 (ㅜ+어 contracts to 워)
사이즈가 안 맞아서 옷을 바꿨어요.
The size didn't fit, so I exchanged the clothes.
-아서 gives the reason; the target size would take -(으)로
자리를 좀 바꿔 주세요.
Could you switch seats with me?
Real request on a train/plane; 바꿔 주세요 asks the other person to do the swap
nuance: 바꾸다 means to replace one thing with another, or to alter something into a different state — money (돈을 바꾸다), seats (자리를 바꾸다), plans (계획을 바꾸다), even your mind (마음을 바꾸다). The dividing line from 고치다 is essential: 바꾸다 ends with a DIFFERENT thing, 고치다 keeps the SAME thing repaired. Returning a defective shirt for a new one is 옷을 바꾸다; mending the torn seam is 옷을 고치다. The destination of the change takes the particle -(으)로: 작은 걸로 바꿔 주세요 ('change it for the small one'). Note also 바뀌다, the intransitive twin: 바꾸다 is 'I change X' (transitive, takes 을/를), while 바뀌다 is 'X changes by itself' (신호등이 바뀌었어요 = 'the light changed') — mixing these up is a frequent error. Conjugation is regular: 바꾸 + 어요 → 바꿔요, past 바꿨어요. English-speaker pitfall: 'change my mind' is 마음을 바꾸다, not 생각을 고치다, and 'change clothes (get dressed)' is 옷을 갈아입다, not 옷을 바꾸다.

Saying 옷을 바꾸다 for 'change clothes/get changed' — that's 옷을 갈아입다; 옷을 바꾸다 means exchange the garment at a store.

usage: the cognate-object pattern: the noun 그림 ('picture') pairs with its verb 그리다 — 그림을 그려요
약도 = a quick hand-drawn map for directions; very common with 그리다
그리다 covers lines and shapes by hand; 선을 그어요 with 긋다 is also used for ruling a straight line
잘 ('well') goes right before the verb: 그림을 잘 그려요 ('I draw well')
examples: 그림을 그려요.
I draw a picture.
Core sentence; stem 그리 + 어요 → 그려요 (이+어 contracts to 여)
아이가 강아지를 그렸어요.
The child drew a puppy.
Past tense 그렸어요; the thing drawn takes -을/를
여기에 간단한 약도를 그려 주세요.
Please draw a simple map here.
여기에 marks the surface with -에 ('onto here'); 그려 주세요 requests the favor
nuance: 그리다 means to draw or depict by hand — pictures, sketches, lines, maps (그림을 그리다, 약도를 그리다), and figuratively even to picture something in your mind (미래를 그리다, 'envision the future'). Keep it apart from 쓰다, which is 'to write' letters, words, and text: 글씨를 쓰다 vs 그림을 그리다 — Koreans firmly split writing from drawing, whereas English 'draw' and 'write' both involve a pen. Also distinguish 칠하다 ('to color in / paint a surface', 색을 칠하다) and 긋다 ('to rule a straight line', 줄을 긋다, a ㅅ-irregular). 그리다 itself is a regular 이-stem verb: 그리 + 어요 contracts to 그려요, past 그렸어요. The main English-speaker pitfall is using 쓰다 by analogy for drawing a diagram or 그리다 for writing your name — write your name is 이름을 쓰다, draw a diagram is 그림을/도표를 그리다. Note a homophone caution: 그리다 also exists poetically meaning 'to long for/miss' (그리워하다 is the everyday form), but in daily life 그리다 = draw.

usage: 부르다 = summon someone/something to come; 택시를 불러 주세요 ('please call a taxi')
the fixed idiom for singing — never 노래를 하다 in this sense; 노래를 불러요
to call out a name to get attention: 선생님이 이름을 불렀어요
a SEPARATE adjective 부르다 meaning 'full' — 배가 불러요 ('I'm full'), not the 'call' verb
examples: 택시를 불러요.
I call a taxi.
르-irregular in action: 부르 + 어요 drops ㅡ and doubles ㄹ → 불러요, never 부르어요
사람이 안 와서 큰 소리로 불렀어요.
Nobody came, so I called out loudly.
큰 소리로 ('in a loud voice') uses -(으)로 for manner; past 불렀어요
우리 같이 노래를 부를까요?
Shall we sing a song together?
부를까요? proposes singing; before 을 the stem stays 부르- (no doubling) → 부를
nuance: 부르다 chiefly means to call/summon someone to come (택시를 부르다, 친구를 부르다), to call out a name (이름을 부르다), and — a key idiom — to sing (노래를 부르다, the standard phrase, not 노래를 하다). Don't confuse it with 전화하다, which is 'to phone': 친구를 불러요 means call your friend over to where you are, while 친구한테 전화해요 means ring them up. It's a textbook 르-irregular: before an 아/어 ending the final ㅡ drops and an extra ㄹ appears, so 부르 + 어요 → 불러요 and past → 불렀어요, but before consonant endings it stays whole (부르고, 부를 거예요, 부릅니다). Two traps: first, learners say 부르어요 — wrong, it must be 불러요. Second, beware the homonym 부르다 'to be full' (배가 부르다), a completely different adjective; 배가 불러요 means 'I'm full', not 'the stomach calls'. Also note honorific contexts: to summon a superior you'd soften with 모시다 ('escort/bring respectfully') rather than bluntly 부르다.

usage: 고르다 = pick one from several physical options; 선물을 골라요
to choose the one you like
마음에 들다 ('to be to one's liking') + 고르다 is a natural pair
deciding what to order: 메뉴를 골랐어요 ('I chose what to eat')
the number/quantity you select takes -을/를: 둘 중에 하나를 골라요 ('pick one of the two')
examples: 옷을 골라요.
I choose clothes.
르-irregular: 고르 + 아요 drops ㅡ and doubles ㄹ → 골라요, never 고르아요
가게에서 예쁜 옷을 골랐어요.
I picked out pretty clothes at the store.
가게에서 uses -에서 for the place of action; past 골랐어요
종류가 너무 많아서 못 골라요.
There are too many kinds, so I can't choose.
못 골라요 ('can't choose'); -아서 expresses the cause
nuance: 고르다 means to choose by picking one (or some) out of a concrete set of options laid before you — clothes on a rack, gifts in a shop, items on a menu. The fine line versus 선택하다 (選擇, a Sino-Korean synonym) is register and abstraction: 고르다 is everyday and hands-on ('grab that one'), while 선택하다 is more formal/written and fits weighty or abstract choices (진로를 선택하다, 'choose a career path'). It also differs from 정하다/결정하다 ('decide, settle'): you 골라요 among visible things, but you 정해요 a date or a plan. As a 르-irregular, before 아/어 the ㅡ drops and ㄹ doubles: 고르 + 아요 → 골라요, past 골랐어요; before consonants it's intact (고르고, 고를게요, 고릅니다). The headline pitfall is 고르아요 (wrong) for 골라요. Also, English 'choose to do something' (a course of action) is NOT 고르다 — say -기로 하다/결정하다; 고르다 needs a tangible thing as its object.

structuredNuance.t: To choose by picking one (or some) out of a concrete set of options laid before you — clothes on a rack, gifts in a shop, items on a menu.

The fine line versus 선택하다 (選擇, a Sino-Korean synonym) is register and abstraction: 고르다 is everyday and hands-on ('grab that one'), while 선택하다 is more formal/written and fits weighty or abstract choices (진로를 선택하다, 'choose a career path'). It also differs from 정하다/결정하다 ('decide, settle'): you 골라요 among visible things, but you 정해요 a date or a plan.
As a 르-irregular, before 아/어 the ㅡ drops and ㄹ doubles: 고르 + 아요 → 골라요, past 골랐어요; before consonants it's intact (고르고, 고를게요, 고릅니다).
The headline pitfall is 고르아요 (wrong) for 골라요. Also, English 'choose to do something' (a course of action) is NOT 고르다 — say -기로 하다/결정하다; 고르다 needs a tangible thing as its object.

mistakes: Saying 고르아요 — as a 르-irregular it becomes 골라요 (ㅡ drops, ㄹ doubles), with past 골랐어요.
Using 고르다 for abstract decisions like a date or plan — use 정하다/결정하다; 고르다 needs concrete options (옷, 선물, 메뉴).
Translating 'choose to do' with 고르다 — 'I chose to stay' is 남기로 했어요, not a 고르다 sentence; 고르다 takes a noun object.

usage: 머리를 잘라요 means cut your hair (often = get it cut at a salon)
the resulting portion takes -(으)로: 반으로 잘라 주세요 ('cut it in half')
자르다 is cutting through with a tool (scissors/knife); 가위로 종이를 잘라요
everyday grooming collocation: 손톱을 잘라요 ('I clip my nails')
examples: 종이를 잘라요.
I cut the paper.
르-irregular: 자르 + 아요 drops ㅡ and doubles ㄹ → 잘라요, never 자르아요
미용실에서 머리를 짧게 잘랐어요.
I got my hair cut short at the salon.
짧게 ('short', adverb) describes how; past 잘랐어요
이 케이크를 반으로 잘라 주세요.
Please cut this cake in half.
반으로 uses -(으)로 for the result; 잘라 주세요 requests the favor
nuance: 자르다 means to cut THROUGH and separate something with a blade or scissors — paper, hair, cake, rope, nails — i.e. to sever into pieces. Distinguish it from 썰다, which is 'to slice' food into many pieces on a board (양파를 썰다, 'chop an onion'), and from 끊다, which is 'to cut off / break' a connection, line, or supply (전화를 끊다 'hang up', 담배를 끊다 'quit smoking') — note 머리를 자르다 (cut hair) but never 머리를 끊다. There's also 깎다 for shaving/peeling/paring (사과를 깎다 'peel an apple', 수염을 깎다 'shave'). It's a 르-irregular: 자르 + 아요 → 잘라요 (ㅡ drops, ㄹ doubles), past 잘랐어요, but consonant endings keep it whole (자르고, 자를게요, 자릅니다). The big pitfall is 자르아요 (wrong) instead of 잘라요. Also, English 'cut prices' or 'cut down' does not map to 자르다 — reducing an amount is 줄이다, and cutting off a service is 끊다.

usage: 정하다 fixes a concrete arrangement; 날짜를 정해요 ('let's decide the date')
장소(場所, 'place') + 정하다 is a standard pairing for planning
정하다 also means 'establish/lay down' rules: 규칙을 정해요
the idiom for settling on a decision internally — 마음을 정했어요
examples: 시간을 정해요.
I set the time.
Single 하다-verb (no separable noun), so it's regular: 정하 + 여요 → 정해요
우리 만날 시간을 먼저 정해요.
Let's decide our meeting time first.
먼저 ('first') sequences the action; 만날 is the future-modifier 'to meet'
아직 휴가 날짜를 못 정했어요.
I haven't been able to decide my vacation dates yet.
아직 + past = 'not yet'; 못 정했어요 ('couldn't decide')
nuance: 정하다 (定하다, 定 'fix/settle') means to settle on and pin down a choice — a date, place, rule, or one's own mind — turning something open into something fixed. Its close synonym 결정하다 (決定, 'decide') leans more formal and weightier (회의에서 결정했어요, 'we decided in the meeting'), whereas 정하다 is the lighter everyday word for arranging plans (시간 정하자, 'let's set a time'). Don't confuse it with 고르다/선택하다 ('choose'): you 골라요 one item from several visible options, but you 정해요 an arrangement or commitment. Unlike the separable noun+하다 verbs (요리하다 → 요리 안 해요), here 정 is bound, so 안/못 go in FRONT: 안 정해요, 못 정해요 — saying 정 안 해요 is wrong. Conjugation: 정하 + 여요 → 정해요, past 정했어요. English-speaker pitfall: 'decide TO do something' is best rendered with -기로 하다 (가기로 했어요, 'decided to go'), not 정하다 alone; 정하다 wants a noun object like 날짜를/장소를.

定하다 — 定 'fix/settle'.

Using 정하다 for 'choose an item' — picking one of several is 고르다/선택하다; 정하다 is for settling an arrangement (date, place, plan).
Saying 가기를 정했어요 for 'I decided to go' — the natural form is 가기로 했어요 (-기로 하다); 정하다 takes a noun, not this clause.

usage: 신청하다 = formally sign up/apply via a form or system; 수업을 신청해요
money/benefits you apply for take -을/를: 장학금을 신청했어요
the means takes -(으)로: 인터넷으로 신청해요 ('apply via the internet')
to fill out an application form
신청서(申請書) is the form itself; you 써요(write) the 신청서 to 신청하다
examples: 수업을 신청해요.
I register for a class.
Noun+하다 compound; the thing applied for takes -을/를, verb 신청해요
인터넷으로 장학금을 신청했어요.
I applied for the scholarship online.
-(으)로 for the method; past 신청했어요
기한이 지나서 지금은 신청 못 해요.
The deadline passed, so I can't apply now.
기한이 지나다 = 'deadline passes'; 못 splits as 신청 못 해요
nuance: 신청하다 (申請하다, 申 'state/report' + 請 'request') means to formally apply, sign up, or put in a request through a proper channel — a class, a card, a scholarship, a subsidy — usually involving a form (신청서) or an online system. Distinguish it carefully from 부탁하다 ('ask a personal favor', 친구한테 부탁해요) and from 지원하다 (志願/支援): 지원하다 is 'apply' for a job or school admission (회사에 지원하다, 'apply to a company'), with a sense of volunteering yourself, whereas 신청하다 is 'apply for / request' a service, slot, or benefit that's offered. As a separable noun+하다 verb, 안/못 wedge before 하다: 신청 안 해요, 신청 못 해요. Conjugation is regular: 신청하 + 여요 → 신청해요, past 신청했어요. English-speaker pitfall: don't use 신청하다 for applying to a job/university — Koreans say 지원하다 there; and don't confuse the everyday 'ask someone to do me a favor' (부탁하다) with the institutional 신청하다.

Distinguish it carefully from 부탁하다 ('ask a personal favor', 친구한테 부탁해요) and from 지원하다 (志願/支援): 지원하다 is 'apply' for a job or school admission (회사에 지원하다, 'apply to a company'), with a sense of volunteering yourself, whereas 신청하다 is 'apply for / request' a service, slot, or benefit that's offered.

mistakes: Using 신청하다 for a job or college application — that's 지원하다 (회사에 지원해요); 신청하다 is for services, classes, cards, benefits.
Confusing it with 부탁하다 — asking a friend for a favor is 부탁하다; 신청하다 is a formal request through a system or form.

usage: 확인하다 = verify/confirm the content; 이메일을 확인해요
확인하다 covers 'confirm something is in order': 예약을 확인했어요
with an embedded question: 맞는지 확인해 주세요 ('check whether it's right')
다시 한번 ('once more') is a stock partner: 다시 한번 확인해 주세요
examples: 이메일을 확인해요.
I check my email.
Noun+하다 compound, regular: stem 확인하 + 여요 → 확인해요
출발하기 전에 시간을 확인해야 해요.
I have to check the time before leaving.
-기 전에 ('before doing'); 확인해야 해요 expresses obligation
이 주소가 맞는지 확인해 주세요.
Please check whether this address is correct.
-는지 embeds the yes/no question; 확인해 주세요 requests the favor
nuance: 확인하다 (確認하다, 確 'certain/firm' + 認 'recognize') means to check, verify, or confirm that something is correct or true — facts, times, reservations, messages — making sure reality matches what you expect. The crucial contrast is with 찾다, which English 'check' can blur: 찾다 is 'to look FOR / search' something not yet located (열쇠를 찾다, 'look for the keys'), whereas 확인하다 is 'to verify' something you can already see (열쇠가 있는지 확인하다, 'check whether the keys are there'). It also differs from 알아보다 ('look into/inquire to find out', 가격을 알아보다). It's a regular noun+하다 verb: 확인하 + 여요 → 확인해요, past 확인했어요, with 안/못 splitting before 하다 (확인 안 해요, 확인 못 해요). English-speaker pitfall: 'check the box' or 'check off' is NOT 확인하다 — ticking a box is 체크하다/표시하다; and 'check out a book/check out (a hotel)' uses 빌리다 or 체크아웃하다, not 확인하다, which strictly means 'verify/confirm'.

It also differs from 알아보다 ('look into/inquire to find out', 가격을 알아보다).

Saying 확인하다 for 'check (tick) a box' — that's 체크하다/표시하다; 확인하다 means confirm/verify, not mark.
Splitting as 못 확인해요 — the standard negative for a noun+하다 verb is 확인 못 해요 / 확인 안 해요.

usage: 취소하다 undoes a booking/order; 예약을 취소해요
online shopping staple: 주문을 취소했어요 ('I canceled the order')
약속(promise/appointment) + 취소하다 — calling off a plan with someone
수수료('fee') pairs with 취소 as a noun phrase you'll meet when canceling bookings
examples: 예약을 취소해요.
I cancel the reservation.
Noun+하다 compound, regular: stem 취소하 + 여요 → 취소해요
일이 생겨서 약속을 취소했어요.
Something came up, so I canceled the appointment.
일이 생기다 = 'something comes up'; -아서 gives the reason; past 취소했어요
이미 결제해서 지금은 취소 못 해요.
I already paid, so I can't cancel now.
이미 ('already') + past reason; 못 splits as 취소 못 해요
nuance: 취소하다 (取消하다, 取 'take' + 消 'extinguish/erase') means to cancel — to call off or undo something already arranged: a reservation, an order, an appointment, a plan. The neat way to remember it: it's the natural opposite of 예약하다/신청하다 (book/apply). Distinguish it from 그만두다, which is 'to quit/stop' an ongoing activity or job (회사를 그만두다, 'quit the company'; 운동을 그만두다, 'stop exercising'): you 취소해요 a future arrangement, but you 그만둬요 something already in progress. It also differs from 미루다 ('postpone', 약속을 미루다, push the appointment later rather than scrap it) — canceling removes it, postponing reschedules it. As a noun+하다 verb it's regular: 취소하 + 여요 → 취소해요, past 취소했어요, with 안/못 before 하다 (취소 안 해요, 취소 못 해요). English-speaker pitfall: 'cancel my subscription / unsubscribe' is more often 해지하다 (解止, end a contract) than 취소하다, and don't use 취소하다 for 'quit a job' — that's 그만두다.
